title: External Drone Auditing
text:
I wanted to combine what I’d learned with the power of the DJI Mini 3 Pro. Although my drone has no imaging capabilities (other than stunning 4K video at 30 frames a second…) in combination with owning an Apple phone, meant I had to do everything myself manually. I had to designate my own flight path, tie points, and determine how many photos were enough to get an accurate 3D model to assess exterior damage… which I called an external audit.























Because of the rising costs in our everyday lives given Trump’s tariff era, I decided to focus my attention to homeowners in the DFW area. As you already might know my parents own this property in Highland Park, what you might not already know is that this area sees a lot of draft coming from the alley placed behind it. Given this information we receive a lot of wind damage to our composition shingles (more known as asphalt shingles). Roofing repairs used to cost us around 500 dollars a visit from our previous installer but given the rising rates due to tariffs (I know this because in the email we get from our roofer there is a disclaimer at the bottom to let you know that tariffs might affect pricing. We received a quote from the same employer for around 1800 making that a 260% increase from 500. Installing a new roof isn’t an option for us as we have new tenants moving in soon and we don’t possess the temporal equity to be able to move forward with that big an endeavor.









These shingles contain toxic metals such as Manganese, Copper, Zinc, Lead, and other harmful chemicals not to mention the petroleum and oil that goes into making these items for commercial usage. Another issue with this method of roofing is the breakdown of the chemical links between the products that make up these shingles from UV rays (the sun). As they breakdown they start to loosen and lose their integrity with the nails and eventually fall off. In tandem with rainwater leaking into the roof, you also see the PH levels rise in the coming days where rainfall is observed (Check out this study: Roofing as a source of non point water pollution – Science Direct). As a result, there is bio accumulation of lead and copper which are both toxic to the environment. And in particular, “However, mean Mn2+ concentrations in runoff from wood and composition shingle roofs were found to be significantly greater than in runoff from painted aluminum or galvanized roofs. (Which at higher quantities can be toxic to the environment)”. According to this roofing website: The Most Popular Roofing Materials in DFW | Dallas Roofing Experts, asphalt shingles are some of the most common roofing methods in the DFW metropolex which renders a concerning idea that we are polluting the environment whether we like it or not.









My goal with this project is to see if I can generate 3D models simply using a camera drone that isn’t necessarily built for jobs of this nature. With the growing interest in UASs I believe soon they will be akin to phones; in that they will be a necessity to keep up with modern technology. According to this site, Drone Market Size 2020-2025 | Drone Industry Insights written by an aerospace engineer, the drone market has increased by nearly 23 billion dollars since 2020 and is only going to go higher. With this significant growth we are going to see drones become more and more a part of our daily lives, including this masterful piece of machinery: Facility Inspection - Oil and Gas - Inspection - DJI Enterprise. Like mailboxes, what if docking stations were a part of standard life? Cutting out the time it takes for inspectors to get out in the field, getting accurate estimates of property YOU own, creating visualizations with a homeowners app in an instant. I believe this kind of change is imminent, which would allow us to take responsibility of our part in environmental sustainability.























I tried to replicate that flight path of the automated app we used in class, but I found for that specific building it wouldn’t quite work with such an intimate area. So, I created an optimal flight path to adjust to my situation. The red dots you see on the right are uncalibrated images that were excluded from the 3D model building process due to being error prone from the angle being too flat and me breaking the homogenous overlap that I had originally created.
















Typically speaking with rendering 3D models, you want your RMSE to be as low as possible concerning the distribution of your tie points. Tie points are common visual features like corners, edges, or texture features that standout to Drone2Map that it can recognize and make a tie point at. The higher number of tie points you have the better your image is going to look, but it comes with the drawback of more storage, more data, and more time till completion. After the tie points are created you get solution points which are essentially those tie points bundled and adjusted (adjusted meaning camera orientation, angle, position, etc.…). My processing time originally was a lot longer after I got errors in my bottom few pictures, so instead of rendering the model with all 176 image I cut out about 10 to relieve those errors and complete the run time. The graph on the right is essentially a cross-match map that displays similar information to the graph on the left, showing tie points and their intersections.









I thought that this was a fabulous looking model and a great output for what this project is trying to accomplish. Now that we live in this digital world, receiving your mail by car and mailbox is outdated anyway, correct? Imagine converting that wasted space into docking stations for all houses in neighborhood to get accurate assessments of structural damage. If that gets too expensive, imagine each neighborhood having its own designated drone to fly around and collect all sorts of vegetation health data, roof structure, wall integrity reports, and any other information under the sun that can be gathered by UAS to save the environment. Battery operated machinery that is cost effective in the long run and can accomplish a plethora of tasks to save us from destroying the Earth sounds like a win to me.























I later discovered on my trip that archaeologists had used drones with imaging capabilities to assess damage over time done to Macchu Picchu. So I’m making an effort to go in the Remote Sensing direction with respect to the Vilcanota mountains. Although my final decision hasn’t been finalized, with the help of my 3D Data Capture / LiDAR class, I hope to be able to narrow my scope soon. More to be added as it develops…

If you’re like me, you were born in the United States, but don’t quite feel like you’re at home.
Every chance I get I make an attempt to travel to places I’ve never seen before. Whether its backpacking through Europe with a buddy of mine, visiting my parents in Portugal, or going North to Canada to stop by for Christmas with my Oma, I’m always looking for a new adventure. Recently, after completing my second semester at UTD I had the idea to visit my study area for one of my final projects for my advanced GIS class. I booked a flight and found myself roaming the streets of Cusco Peru and had started my two week solo adventure in South America. My goal was to experience a different culture as well as try and grab relevant data with my DJI Mini 3 Pro for potential thesis data (Peru have very strict drone laws…), but ultimately I was there to feel small again. After visiting many different cities and historical sites I finally found myself at the biggest attraction, Macchu Picchu. At only 24 I had reached one of the World’s wonders and had the chance to explore this ancient relic of time, and also came to the conclusion that there’s so much more to see in this World than just Texas. I want to use the knowledge I’m accumulating from this masters and put it into practice all over the world…

library(haven)
TEDS_2016 <- read_stata("https://github.com/datageneration/home/blob/master/DataProgramming/data/TEDS_2016.dta?raw=true")
regplot <- function(x, y, var_name = "Variable") {
  # Remove NAs so the model and plot align
  df_clean <- na.omit(data.frame(x = x, y = y))
  
  fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_clean)

  plot(jitter(df_clean$x), jitter(df_clean$y), 
       pch = 19, 
       col = rgb(0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.3), # Transparent blue
       xlab = var_name, 
       ylab = "Dependent Variable (Tondu)",
       main = paste("Regression: Tondu vs", var_name))
  abline(fit, col = "red", lwd = 3)
  
  return(summary(fit))
}

title: Scraping Government Data
text:
Using the script provided with minor adjustments, downloading one to five documents at a time takes a minuscule amount of time. Whether you have pre-made CSV, JSON file makes the process a lot easier and more manageable especially if those files are specific and as detailed as they were for us making running this script fairly simple.
However, running the script that downloads ALL documents from the https://www.govinfo.gov/ is not a feasible way of scraping data especially if those pdf files are going to retain their size with all of the unnecessary information remaining in those documents (unnecessary information being distinguished by the web scraper for whichever goal you’re trying to achieve). My start time today running the script was 2:31PM and my end time was 3:01PM. So in 30 minutes I managed to download around one thousand pdf files that I have still to go through and dictate necessary information from unnecessary information. If the goal of this script was to scrape every document on a website that meets a specific criteria then that goal has been achieved and the script has served its purpose. But… If you were trying to gather all information on a specific topic and you didn’t have access to these ready made CSV/JSON files, this is not a feasible way of sifting through all the documentation. I would prefer keyword searches using third party applications, or tweaking this script to gather a more manageable data set that is readable unlike the hundreds of pdf files that I now have to manually go through in order for the script to retain some sort of value.

title: Weekly Reflections
text:
In my experience using AI and observing how others use AI as a part of the OIT team at UTD, it has become an all encompassing tool for students to tackle any kind of project that they may encounter during their studies here at the University. At times relied on too much, artificial intelligence will inevitably be integrated into our daily lives at one point or another… In my opinion it’s important for users to understand certain things…



It’s imperative, that users understand that once certain LLMs take in PII, you are essentially forfeiting your privacy…
LLMs should be used as supplemental knowledge and not the basis for claims, actionable knowledge, or a primary source. These models are drawing from elsewhere anyways which, not only excludes it form being a primary source, but should be carefully vetted if that information is going to be passed on to something/somebody else.
Multiple models should be used especially for items such as peer review or journal articles. As predictive outputs have been found to make up unfinished articles and lay claims to somethings that haven’t been studied, but will be investigated, but is present in said articles.




AI isn’t quite at the turning point to which it will completely erase originality in terms artistic or creative ability. A somewhat solid rebuttal to this effect is sculpting, pottery, or architecture, which are artisanal fields that still exist in today’s day and age alongside machinery that can pretty much sculpt better than Donatello… To that point, I would like to believe that most educated people can come to the conclusion that things have been AI doctored the same way they can tell that things have been machine made. Making hand crafted goods, or these previously mentioned “artisanal fields” still very much desirable goods/services.
As for Artificial General Intelligence, my thoughts are somewhat similar to the argument that I’m making above, in that even though LLMs might be able to convey human reasoning to some degree (my brain instantly goes to therapy or psychology in these matters) the beauty in most previously written works that have been bestowed upon the human race in some form of knowledge is the “human factor”. Being able to have multiple perspectives can lead to innovation and inquiry that I suppose only comes from different minds. I can read Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations before I go to sleep at night and might gather some different idea from his anecdotal perspective of stoicism than someone else might. I don’t think AGI (in this current day and age) will be able to appropriately convey that sentiment.






There are a couple of ways off the top of my head that I can think of, for example:
A. Citation machine
B. Summarization of large documents to which don’t pertain to my field (potentially gaining an understanding from the perspective of someone in that field)
C. Ping Pong Partner (A lot of times I use it in terms of a wall I can bounce ideas off of)
D. Initialization (I find the beginning of my journey when writing things is the most difficult part, and it’s nicer to build off a foundation rather than staring at a blank page)
For these purposes I will probably be using a combination of Gemini, Claude, and Microsoft’s CoPilot as we have easy access via the University.






One can think of data, information, knowledge, and wisdom as a hierarchy of sorts…
Data (either discovered or found) translated -> into information, which makes sense of the raw data -> an accumulation of information develops actionable insights that might be of use (or not, which one could argue - the most classic example being, “you didn’t fail to make something 1,000 times you just figured out how to not make something 1,000 times - is similar in this event) turns into knowledge -> and eventually an accumulation of said”knowledge” bank leads to wisdom, which is experience. Deriving my thoughts from my studies and this class I would say that the difference between information and knowledge is easily translatable to something like this:

Raw Data -> Cake Ingredients
Information -> Recipe
Knowledge -> The Technique (required to make the cake)
Wisdom -> Mastery Experience to the craft
All in all, it’s important to understand the four levels of curiosity displayed in this analogy which are: what = raw data, who/where/when = information, how = knowledge, and the last but arguably the most important, why = wisdom.




In my past experience (and I’ll preface this next thought here that I DID NOT USE AI FOR THESE OPINIONS, which I feel is important to mention when speaking on a subject such as this one) using AI for an assortment of things, one could argue that there’s a plethora of different responses that you can get from prompting an LLM especially in regards to high level questions that you might needs answers to. I would also argue the field of GIS is a pretty niche field in relation to others and when prompting it questions I might have when using certain programs it definitely reaches and delivers hallucinations at times especially when the specificity gets narrower. One of my group members in class also happened to mention the fact that Gemini remembers inputs you might have previously used, and even when starting new chats it will still make callbacks to some of those inputs, which in regards to commonsensical things is extremely frustrating because the problem you’re trying to solve might have slight differences or calls for “niche” responses.

In Finance, the focus has shifted to high-fidelity fraud detection and automated compliance. The Behavioral Hypothesis
To understand the psychological shift accompanying this technological surge, we can formulate the following hypothesis:

The Cognitive Offloading Hypothesis: As ML agents transition from “assistants” (providing suggestions) to “decision-makers” (executing actions), human users will experience a decrease in cognitive agency and critical skepticism, leading to an “automation bias” where the machine’s output is accepted as an objective truth rather than a statistical probability.

Key Factors Influencing Future Behavior
Several factors will dictate how our behavior reshapes around these intelligent systems:

The “Convenience vs. Agency” Trade-off: As ML handles routine decisions (e.g., email drafting, financial planning, or scheduling), people may lose the “mental muscles” required for these tasks. This leads to cognitive atrophy, where individuals become overly reliant on algorithmic nudges for complex life choices.
Algorithmic Polarization: Recommendation engines create feedback loops. In the future, behavior may become more predictable—and thus more easily manipulated—as users are continuously fed content that reinforces existing biases, narrowing the scope of human curiosity.
Trust and Transparency (XAI): The adoption of Explainable AI (XAI) will be the pivot point. If systems remain “black boxes,” public behavior may be driven by skepticism or fear. Conversely, if ML can explain its “why,” we may see a future of Human-AI Symbiosis, where people use AI to augment their intuition rather than replace it.
The Rise of the “Human Premium”: As ML automates technical and analytical tasks, human behavior will likely shift toward prioritizing soft skills—empathy, ethical judgment, and creative strategy—values that remain difficult for models to replicate authentically.

Machine learning (ML) has moved from a specialized research field into a foundational technology embedded across real-world domains, shaping decisions, automating processes, and influencing human behavior. At its core, ML refers to algorithms that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed. Its practical applications span healthcare, finance, transportation, retail, and public policy, often operating invisibly in everyday life.
In healthcare, ML models analyze medical images, predict disease risks, and personalize treatment plans. For example, supervised learning systems trained on labeled datasets can detect anomalies in radiology scans with accuracy comparable to human specialists. In finance, ML is widely used for fraud detection, credit scoring, and algorithmic trading. These systems continuously adapt to new data, identifying subtle behavioral patterns that indicate risk. Transportation has been transformed by ML through route optimization, demand forecasting, and the development of autonomous vehicles, which rely heavily on computer vision and reinforcement learning. Retail platforms use recommendation systems—powered by collaborative filtering and deep learning—to personalize user experiences and influence purchasing behavior. Governments and organizations also deploy ML for resource allocation, predictive policing, and disaster response planning.
A testable hypothesis emerging from these applications is: As machine learning systems become more personalized and predictive, individuals will increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendations over independent decision-making, leading to measurable shifts in autonomy and preference formation.
This hypothesis can be empirically evaluated by observing behavioral changes in environments where ML systems are introduced or enhanced. For instance, A/B testing on recommendation systems can measure how users’ choices diverge when exposed to algorithmic suggestions versus neutral interfaces. Longitudinal studies could assess whether repeated reliance on ML-driven recommendations reduces exploratory behavior or diversity in choices over time.
Several key factors are likely to influence how people behave in an ML-driven future:

Trust and Transparency: Users are more likely to adopt and rely on ML systems when they perceive them as accurate and fair. Explainable AI—systems that provide understandable reasons for their outputs—can increase trust and reduce resistance.
Data Privacy Concerns: As ML systems depend on large volumes of personal data, concerns about surveillance and misuse may shape user behavior. Stricter regulations or high-profile data breaches could reduce willingness to engage with ML-powered services.
Algorithmic Bias and Fairness: If ML systems reinforce existing social biases, affected populations may distrust or reject them. Addressing fairness in model design is critical for widespread acceptance.
Convenience vs. Control Trade-off: ML often offers convenience by automating decisions, but at the cost of user control. Individuals vary in their tolerance for this trade-off, influencing adoption rates.
Digital Literacy: Understanding how ML systems work can affect how people interact with them. Higher literacy may lead to more critical engagement, while lower literacy may increase passive reliance.
Economic Incentives: Businesses design ML systems to optimize engagement and profit, which can subtly steer user behavior. Pricing strategies, nudges, and personalized marketing all play roles.

In conclusion, machine learning is not just a technical tool but a behavioral force. Its growing integration into daily life will likely reshape how people make decisions, interact with systems, and perceive autonomy. The balance between utility, ethics, and human agency will determine its long-term societal impact.

Real-World Domains
Healthcare is one of ML’s most transformative frontiers. Algorithms trained on millions of medical images can detect cancers, diabetic retinopathy, and cardiovascular anomalies with accuracy that rivals — and in some narrow tasks, surpasses — specialist clinicians. Predictive models also flag patients at risk of sepsis or readmission, allowing earlier, cheaper interventions.
Finance relies heavily on ML for credit scoring, algorithmic trading, and fraud detection. Models process thousands of transactional signals in milliseconds to approve a loan or flag a suspicious charge, replacing heuristic rule sets that were slower and easier to game.
Transportation is undergoing a structural shift. Autonomous vehicle systems use convolutional neural networks to interpret sensor data in real time, while logistics companies like UPS and FedEx use route-optimization models to save millions of miles driven annually — reducing cost and emissions simultaneously.
Agriculture has embraced precision ML tools that analyze satellite imagery, soil composition, and weather patterns to prescribe irrigation and fertilization at the individual-plant level, dramatically improving yield while reducing resource waste.
Criminal justice and public policy represent more contentious territory. Predictive policing tools and recidivism risk scores are deployed widely, though their use raises serious concerns about entrenched bias — a domain where ML’s risks are as visible as its benefits.

A Tested Hypothesis
Hypothesis: The more frequently individuals receive personalized ML-driven outputs — recommendations, diagnostics, financial nudges — the more they will defer to algorithmic judgment over their own intuition, even in high-stakes personal decisions.
This hypothesis is supported by behavioral research. Studies in algorithm aversion and appreciation show a nuanced picture: people initially distrust algorithms but, after repeated positive experiences with accurate predictions, shift toward over-reliance — a phenomenon called automation bias. Experiments in medical decision-support contexts have confirmed that clinicians shown an AI recommendation frequently anchor to it, even when the recommendation is demonstrably wrong.

Key Factors Influencing Future Human Behavior
Several forces will determine how deeply ML reshapes human agency:

Explainability. As “black box” models give way to interpretable AI, people may calibrate trust more accurately — relying on ML where it excels and retaining judgment where it fails.
Personalization depth. The more granular the model’s knowledge of an individual, the stronger its influence over that person’s choices, preferences, and perceived needs.
Regulatory environment. Legislation like the EU AI Act introduces mandatory transparency requirements, which could slow adoption in sensitive domains but build longer-term public trust.
Digital literacy. Populations with higher ML literacy are better equipped to interrogate outputs, reducing blind deference and demanding accountability from deploying institutions.
Economic incentive structures. When companies profit from engagement and conversion, ML systems will be optimized to influence behavior, not merely inform it — a tension that will define the next decade of human-computer interaction.

The trajectory is clear: ML will not remain a background utility. It is becoming an active participant in how humans reason, decide, and live.
